parole.significato: A type of lyrical poetry, traditionally Provençal, about lovers who must part at dawn.
parole.testo: First attested in 1821; borrowed from Occitan alba, ultimately from Latin albus (“white”); compare Spanish alba (“dawn”).

parole.significato: Bottarga; a cake or sausage made from salted mullet roe.
parole.testo: From Occitan boutargo, from Arabic بُطَارِخ (buṭāriḵ). Doublet of bottarga and tarek.

parole.significato: A thick heavy fabric into which raised patterns have been woven, originally in gold and silver; more recently any cloth…
parole.testo: From Occitan brocada and Spanish and Portuguese brocado, influenced by French brocart, from Italian broccato, from brocco, ultimately from Gaulish.

parole.significato: One of the teeth used by a carnivore for shearing flesh, being the last upper premolar and the first lower molar.
parole.testo: From French carnass(ier) (“carnivorous”) + -ial, from Occitan carnassa, from carn + -assa (feminine form of Occitan -às), from Latin carn- + -āceus.

parole.significato: A shape-shifting water sprite, imp, or malevolent demon that haunts rivers.
parole.testo: From Occitan, from Latin dracō (“dragon”), from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn, “dragon”).

parole.significato: A sandwich originating in southern France, composed of Niçoise salad in a circular bun.
parole.testo: Occitan pan (“bread”) + banhat (“wet”), past participle of banhar.

parole.significato: A female composer of Old Occitan lyric poetry; a female troubadour.
The shady side of a mountain; in the northern hemisphere, this is typically the north-facing slope.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan ubac, from Latin opācus. Doublet of opaque.
Derived from Italian cicala and Occitan cicala. Doublet of cicada.

parole.significato: A simple saddle girth used in Mexico.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan cencha, from Latin cincta, or from Spanish cincha (“a belt or girth”), from Late Latin cingula, from Latin cingulum. Doublet of cingle.
